research.open_territory:
The niche splits into three naming camps and leaves the middle empty. (1) Generic labels: Crime + adjective, FBI + verb, X Files, Investigation, Best Documentary. They describe the topic but can't be owned, and every literal crime noun I probed (Underworld, Gangland, Crime Empire, The Racket, Street Files, Heist Files, Kingpin Stories, Cartel Chronicles, Mob Stories, Omerta, The Takedown, Syndicate) came back TAKEN. (2) Street-slang and host-name channels (Trap Lore Ross, Hood Edition, Block Archives, The Connect, Tommy G). Their register glamorises the life, which this channel must avoid. (3) Generalist documentary imprints with short abstract names (fern, Lume, Soft White Underbelly). They win the biggest views, which shows that a non-literal, ownable name works when the packaging is strong. Nobody in street-level and organised crime owns a premium imprint name of that kind.

Open imagery nobody uses:
(a) The working-class physical world the crews came from and operated in, in plain concrete nouns: night shifts, loading docks, freight yards, waterfronts, overpasses, sodium streetlights, the corner, the count room, toolboxes and workwear. This gives grit and humanity without menace words.
(b) The investigator's and court's paper trail beyond the worn-out 'files': surveillance logs, the proffer and the cooperator, the docket, the exhibit, the indictment's language. This matches the brief's research-led tone and its informants-and-betrayal angle, and nobody in the niche uses legal vocabulary as a brand.
(c) Metaphors of slow build and collapse from nature or material: fault lines, undertow, rust, embers, tinder, cracks spreading through concrete. These fit the series shape (origins, expansion, betrayal, collapse) and stay grounded rather than sensational.

The name should also sit apart from the sister channels. Channel 12 will draw on finance vocabulary (ledgers, balance sheets) and channel 13 on elite and power vocabulary (dynasty, empire, syndicate). This channel's register should therefore be blue-collar, tactile and human. It should also avoid channel 7's antique-archive lightness, so no 'archive', 'files' or old-paper conceits. Avoid 'narco', 'trap', 'hood' and similar loaded or slang words, which also read badly in Spanish.

table.name: Until Someone Talked
table.why: Handle @UntilSomeoneTalked (18). Sounds like the last line of a crew's story: it ran for years until someone talked. That covers the informant-and-betrayal turning point that most of these stories hinge on, and the past tense reads as documentary. Human and tense, with no slang, no menace words and no glamour. Fine in Spanish ('hasta que alguien habló'). It sets a mood rather than promising an informant in every episode. Small risk: a channel already holds @SomebodyAlwaysTalks (TAKEN in my check), so secure @UntilSomebodyTalked as well. Score 8.5.

by_lens.reason: My full check came back CLEAR (YouTube clear, .com available, no live US marks), and a web search found no book, show or podcast with this title. It's the only candidate that carries the series arc: a crew that ran for years, then a betrayal, then the fall. It sounds human and tense, doesn't glamorise anything, and the past tense reads as documentary. A true-crime viewer gets 'talked = informant' at once, and the name stands apart from the many 'X and Y' names across the portfolio. Two weaknesses. 'Someone' and 'somebody' are easy to swap when heard once: my run showed Somebody Talked and Someone Talked both TAKEN on YouTube, while @UntilSomebodyTalked was CLEAR, so secure that handle too. And it doesn't name crews outright, so the logo and tagline have to do that.

My brandcheck: CLEAR (YouTube CLEAR, untilsomeonetalked.com available, 0 live US marks). The likeliest mishearing is someone/somebody: 'Until Somebody Talked' was CLEAR in my ytcheck, so secure it too. 'Someone Talked' and 'Somebody Talked' came back TAKEN, but only by tiny channels. No video owns the exact phrase in search. It's easy to type in US and UK accents, and the past tense reads as documentary. It carries the series arc (it ran until it collapsed), with no slang, menace or glamour, and it's fine in Spanish. Small risks: it signals crime and secrets in general rather than street crews in particular, so it could also fit channels 12 or 13. It also leans on informant ('snitch') framing, so episodes should not be built around naming cooperators. It's the only candidate here with real spark.

research.open_territory:
The niche splits four ways. Legacy news brands (WSJ, Bloomberg Originals, FRONTLINE, DW, Insider). Personal-name investigators (Coffeezilla, Patrick Boyle, Hamish Hodder, Joe Bartolozzi, Nick Shirley). One-word faceless documentary brands (fern, Lume, Gloam, Crumb, Brew), which are strong but say nothing about money. A long tail of small channels that stack the same literal words: Files, Exposed, Greed, Fraud, Empire, Hidden, Capital, Wealth, Lies, Decoded. No channel owns a calm, premium, finance-specific name that sounds like a documentary label rather than a clickbait feed. That is the main gap, and the brief's tone (sharp, forensic, clear about money) fits it.

My checks show bare idioms and bare single jargon words are gone as handles: Paper Trail, Follow the Money, Cooked Books, Off the Books, Shell Game, Fine Print, Smoke and Mirrors, Red Flags, Red Ink, Tick Mark, Going Concern and Restatement are all TAKEN. Open names will be fresh two-word pairings, not stock phrases.

Imagery nobody in the niche uses:
(1) Physical money and its paper as evidence, the forensic accountant's view: the wire, the watermark, the signature, the seal, the stub, the carbon copy, the footnote, the decimal point, the audit opinion, the vault, the ticker tape.
(2) Old forms of money fraud as metaphor: coin clipping, debasement, counterfeit, alloy, gilt over lead, the false bottom, the scale with a thumb on it. All read as financial deception without saying 'fraud' or 'scam'.
(3) Exposure as a precise instrument rather than 'Exposed': cutting, weighing, assaying, x-raying, holding a note up to the light. This matches 'forensic'. Avoid 'Lens' (Crime Lens) and 'Decoded'.
(4) Measured, literary tone: a name that could sit on a book spine or a film studio card, which none of the small competitors attempt.

Constraints for sister channels: channel 11 (blue-collar crime) and channel 13 (organised crime) need devices of their own. Avoid a shared 'Files' / 'Dossier' / 'Chronicles' / 'Ledger' frame. Channel 13's neighbours already use Dossier Room and Gangland Chronicles. Spanish-speaking viewers see Malditos, Fortunas, Estafa and Fraude everywhere, and 'Heist' calls up La casa de papel. A neutral English coinage that reads cleanly in Spanish is open.

The niche is split between broadcasters with institutional names (FT, Bloomberg, DW, FRONTLINE, OCCRP), on-camera hosts using their own names (Johnny Harris, Tommy G, Franzese), and a long tail of faceless channels that all use the same kit: a genre noun (Mafia/Cartel/Syndicate/Underworld) or a dark adjective (Dark/Black/Shadow/Hidden) plus a container (Files/Ledger/Empire/Vault/Dossier/Chronicles). Unclaimed: (1) The real vocabulary of financial intelligence and investigators' tradecraft (correspondent banking, beneficial ownership, nominees, shells, wires, cables, cut-outs, red notices, the evidence board's link chart). It is cool and precise, signals cross-border money and power rather than street crime, and only Echelon Files and Hidden Ops dabble in it, both crudely. (4) Imagery of elite settings rather than gangland: boardrooms, private banks, embassies, yachts, a seat at the table, the quiet room. It sets the channel apart from street-crime channels (channel 11's lane) and from mafia-romance spam.

On topics, elite money laundering, oligarch networks and kleptocracy are under-served by quality faceless channels. Searches return big outlets plus near-empty AI channels, so a name that signals power + money + crime (rather than 'mafia' or 'cartel') can own the upmarket lane.
